items.prompt: Why should an operation budget be stated explicitly instead of using a universal rule such as "10^8 operations always fit"?

options.text: Actual throughput depends on operation cost, language, hardware, memory behavior, and time limit.
Big-O already gives an exact runtime in seconds.
Variable names determine the machine speed.
Constraints never influence algorithm choice.

feedback.reason: A rough budget is a modeling assumption, not a universal physical constant.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

An operation budget translates a time limit into deliberately simplified units. One hash lookup, cache miss, allocation, comparison, interpreted-language step and vector instruction do not have equal wall-clock cost. Big-O also removes constants and lower-order terms. Therefore a claim such as 10^8 must name its abstract cost model and remain a first-pass filter, not a universal runtime guarantee.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Use the estimate to reject orders-of-magnitude mismatches. Near the boundary, benchmark the relevant implementation or preserve a conservative margin because the abstract units no longer decide the outcome.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.big_o_exact: Asymptotic notation describes growth and intentionally omits the constants, operation costs and platform needed for seconds.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names_determine: Renaming a variable changes no executed instruction, memory access or property of the target machine.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.budget_unneeded: Maximum input sizes determine how often the dominant operation runs and are central to rejecting infeasible candidates.

items.prompt: With n = 200,000 and an abstract budget of 100,000,000 unit operations, which candidate is clearly infeasible by its dominant count?

options.text: An O(n²) full pair comparison.
An O(n) scan.
An O(n log2 n) comparison process.
An O(1) check.

feedback.reason: n² is approximately 40 billion when n = 200,000.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Substitute the maximum input into each dominant count. The quadratic candidate performs (200,000)^2 = 40,000,000,000 pair checks, which is 400 times the 100,000,000-unit budget. In contrast, n is 200,000 and n log2 n is about 200,000 · 18 = 3.6 million. The quadratic gap is already decisive before constant overhead.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: An order-of-magnitude rejection does not require pretending the abstract budget predicts seconds. Forty billion dominant checks cannot be rescued to one hundred million by a modest constant-factor optimization.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear: The dominant count is about 200,000 units, five hundred times below the stated first-pass budget.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_log_n: Using log2 200,000 ≈ 18 gives about 3.6 million units, still well below the abstract budget.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: A fixed number of operations does not grow with n and is smaller than every listed input-dependent candidate here.

constraints: Use an abstract budget of 100,000,000 equal-cost unit operations and ignore constant factors.

items.prompt: With n = 20, what does the size of the full subset space suggest?

options.text: 2^20 is about one million, so complete enumeration may be viable under a suitable per-state cost and budget.
Any exponential algorithm is automatically impossible.
2^20 grows linearly with n.
There are only 20 subsets.

feedback.reason: Asymptotic class alone is not the whole feasibility decision.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Each of 20 elements contributes an include/exclude decision, so the state count is 2^20 = 1,048,576. That is small enough to remain plausible under many explicit budgets if work per state is cheap. The conclusion is conditional: scanning 20 elements per state costs about 21 million steps, and materializing a large output adds its own time and storage.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Exponential growth is a warning about scaling, not an automatic verdict for every concrete n. Always substitute the maximum exponent and then include work and output per state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_impossible: The concrete count here is roughly one million, so feasibility depends on the declared budget and per-state work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear: Adding one element doubles the state space, which is exponential growth rather than adding one more state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.twenty_states: Twenty counts input positions; their independent binary membership choices combine into 2^20 different subsets.

items.prompt: With n = 50, why is enumerating all 2^n subsets normally rejected under a 100,000,000-operation budget?

options.text: 2^50 is over one quadrillion states, far beyond the budget.
The code would probably use nested loops.
Subset enumeration produces no output.
Every algorithm with n = 50 is infeasible.

feedback.reason: The candidate state count itself exceeds the budget by many orders of magnitude.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The loop would visit 2^50 = 1,125,899,906,842,624 masks—over 11 million times the 100,000,000-unit budget—even before decoding or output. This is not a close constant-factor decision. The state count alone rejects complete enumeration under the stated workload, although other polynomial algorithms can be entirely feasible for n = 50.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject on the smallest decisive lower bound. If visiting each candidate once already exceeds the budget by seven orders of magnitude, optimizing the body cannot make full enumeration viable.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.nested_name: Loop syntax does not establish the number of states; the explicit 2^50 count is the decisive evidence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_zero: Enumerating subsets may emit enormous output, and even a visitor that emits nothing must still traverse the stated states.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fifty_large: The number fifty is not inherently infeasible; linear, quadratic and many other polynomial workloads can be small at n = 50.

constraints: Use an abstract budget of 100,000,000 equal-cost unit operations.

items.prompt: An algorithm preprocesses n records in O(n log n) and answers q queries in O(log n) each. Which workload expression should be compared with the budget?

options.text: O(n log n + q log n).
O(log n) only.
O(n log n) only.
O(nq log² n).

feedback.reason: Feasibility is based on the full requested workload.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The phases run sequentially, so their costs add. Preprocessing contributes n log n once, while q queries contribute q · log n. The full dominant workload is therefore n log n + q log n = (n + q) log n under the shared logarithm. Looking only at one query understates repeated work; multiplying preprocessing by q overstates a phase performed once.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Write the lifecycle formula before substituting values: construction + updates + queries + mandatory output. Add sequential phases and multiply a per-operation term only by the number of times that phase executes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.query_only: This is the cost of one query and omits both the q repetitions and the one-time preprocessing phase.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.preprocess_only: Construction is only the first phase; the requested q query operations must also be included in total work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.multiply_all: Preprocessing runs once and queries run afterward, so the phases add rather than multiplying every factor together.

items.prompt: Two input dimensions are n = 10,000 and m = 10,000. What should be checked before accepting an O(nm) nested comparison?

options.text: Compute nm = 100,000,000 and compare it with the stated budget and per-comparison cost.
Rename m to n so the loop looks quadratic.
Use n + m because there are two inputs.
Only the larger dimension matters.

feedback.reason: Multidimensional constraints should be substituted into the actual cost expression.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

An O(nm) comparison examines the Cartesian product of the two dimensions. Substitution gives 10,000 · 10,000 = 100,000,000 comparisons, exactly the abstract boundary before per-comparison overhead. This makes the candidate borderline rather than automatically safe and calls for a realistic constant, memory-access model or measurement.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Keep independent maxima separate until they enter the formula. Replacing n and m with one symbol can hide asymmetric constraints; replacing a product with a sum changes the algorithm being analyzed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rename_m: Renaming m does not change the two loop extents or the 100 million pairs that the algorithm visits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.add_only: n + m counts a pass over each collection, while comparing every cross-collection pair requires their product.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_m: For each of n records the algorithm processes m counterparts, so both independent dimensions multiply the work.

items.prompt: Why can two algorithms with the same Big-O classification differ in feasibility near a tight limit?

options.text: Their constant factors, operation types, memory access, and implementation overhead can differ.
Big-O is never useful for comparing algorithms.
Their variable names may be longer.
Algorithms in the same class always have identical runtime.

feedback.reason: Asymptotic filtering rejects clearly wrong growth classes first.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Big-O groups algorithms by long-run growth, not exact work. Two O(n) implementations may perform one comparison per element versus hashing, allocation and several random memory accesses; two O(n log n) sorts may have different constants and cache behavior. Growth class reliably rejects large-order mismatches, but near a tight limit these hidden factors can decide feasibility.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Use asymptotics first, then refine only surviving near-boundary candidates with operation mix, allocation, locality, language/runtime and representative measurement.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.big_o_wrong: Big-O remains the correct tool for comparing growth and rejecting candidates; it simply is not a stopwatch.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Identifier length has no effect on the compiled or interpreted workload represented by the two algorithms.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_always: Sharing a growth class still permits different constant factors, lower-order work, memory access and runtime overhead.

items.prompt: A task must output k records. Why must k be considered when assessing feasibility?

options.text: Writing or materializing k records requires at least proportional work and usually proportional output storage.
Output is free once the algorithm computes the first record.
Only input size can affect complexity.
k is always constant.

feedback.reason: A candidate time bound smaller than the mandatory output size is incomplete.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

If the contract requires k records, the system must at least visit or write those k outputs, establishing an Ω(k) time lower bound. Returning them simultaneously usually also needs Ω(k) output storage, or more when each record has nonconstant size. An internal search faster than k does not remove the cost of satisfying the external result contract.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Separate computation, emission and retention. Streaming can reduce peak output memory, but it cannot make producing k required records take o(k) time.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_free: Computing the first record does not write the remaining k - 1 required records or pay their serialization cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.input_only: The result can be larger than the input, and mandatory output then supplies the dominant lower bound.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.k_constant: k is a workload quantity that may grow with input constraints, so it cannot be assumed constant without evidence.

items.prompt: A proposed O(n²) dynamic-programming table uses n = 50,000 boolean entries per dimension. Which resource issue appears before runtime details?

options.text: The table has 2.5 billion cells and may exceed the memory budget.
Booleans always occupy zero memory asymptotically.
Only CPU time matters when evaluating constraints.
The table is large only because both dimensions are named n.

feedback.reason: Constraint translation includes memory as well as operations.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The table contains 50,000 · 50,000 = 2,500,000,000 cells. Even at an idealized one byte per boolean, that is about 2.5 GB before row objects, alignment and runtime overhead; wider boolean storage makes it larger. If the memory limit is below that footprint, the representation is rejected before transition speed matters.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Translate space formulas into bytes using the actual representation and include container overhead. A compressed bitset changes the constant substantially, but it must be an implemented representation rather than an assumed rescue.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_constant: Each boolean cell consumes represented storage, so billions of cells cannot occupy asymptotically or physically zero memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_only: An algorithm that cannot allocate its state is infeasible regardless of whether its CPU transitions would finish in time.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names_quadratic: The 2.5 billion-cell product comes from two independent extents, not from the spelling of their variables.

items.prompt: Which quantities should be included when translating constraints into a budget? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maximum values of every independent input dimension.
The number of repeated operations or queries.
The maximum required output volume.
The spelling of loop variables.

feedback.reason: Feasibility follows the complete workload shape.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Every independent maximum must be substituted into the phase where it contributes: input dimensions determine scan or product sizes, query count multiplies per-query work, and required output establishes emission and storage lower bounds. Omitting any one can change the result by orders of magnitude. Variable spelling never enters an operation or byte count.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Build a workload ledger before choosing an algorithm: maximum dimensions, construction, updates, queries, result volume, memory limit and time model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_names: Changing a loop variable's spelling leaves its range, executed operations and memory footprint exactly the same.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.output_size: Output creates an unavoidable lower bound.

items.prompt: Under an abstract 100,000,000-operation budget and n = 100,000, which candidate classes are plausibly viable before constant-factor review? Select all that apply.

options.text: O(n).
O(n log2 n).
O(n²).
O(n³).

feedback.reason: Substituting the maximum n gives a first-pass feasibility filter.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

At n = 100,000, a linear candidate has about 100,000 dominant units and n log2 n has roughly 100,000 · 17 = 1.7 million. Both are comfortably below 100 million before constant review. Quadratic work is 10^10 and cubic work is 10^15, exceeding the abstract budget by factors of 100 and ten million respectively.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Accepting a class here means 'plausible enough for the next review', not guaranteed fast. Constants, memory and output remain part of the final decision.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.quadratic: 100,000 squared is 10 billion dominant units, one hundred times the stated abstract budget.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cubic: 100,000 cubed is 10^15 dominant units, which exceeds the budget by seven orders of magnitude.

constraints: Treat one dominant-count unit as one abstract operation and ignore constant factors.

items.prompt: Which exhaustive spaces can be plausible under a 100,000,000-state budget? Select all that apply.

options.text: All 2^20 subsets.
All 2^26 subsets.
All 2^40 subsets.
All 12! permutations.

feedback.reason: Concrete state counts matter when n is small.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Compute each state space: 2^20 = 1,048,576 and 2^26 = 67,108,864, both below 100 million visits. In contrast, 2^40 ≈ 1.10 trillion and 12! = 479,001,600 exceed it. The accepted counts are only first-pass plausible because work per state and required output may multiply the total.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: For exponential and factorial candidates, substitute the actual small constraint instead of rejecting or accepting solely from the class name.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.subsets_40: 2^40 is about 1.10 trillion states, more than eleven thousand times the 100 million-state budget.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.permutations_12: 12! equals 479,001,600 orderings, already almost five times the budget before processing each one.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.subsets_26: This is about 67 million states before per-state overhead.

constraints: Use an abstract budget of 100,000,000 states before per-state work.

items.prompt: Which caveats belong in an operation-budget estimate? Select all that apply.

options.text: The estimate treats operations as abstract equal-cost units.
Constant factors and cache behavior may matter near the limit.
Memory and output constraints may reject an otherwise acceptable operation count.
The estimate proves every implementation finishes in the same wall-clock time.

feedback.reason: A good estimate states what it includes and what remains uncertain.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

An honest estimate declares that its units abstract unequal real operations, preserves constant and cache uncertainty near the boundary, and checks memory plus mandatory output independently. It can justify rejecting a clearly oversized candidate or selecting one for measurement, but it cannot prove identical wall-clock time across languages, hardware and implementations.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: State both the conclusion and its confidence boundary: decisive order-of-magnitude rejection, plausible with margin, or benchmark required.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.universal_speed: Different operation costs, runtimes and machines invalidate any claim that one abstract count guarantees identical elapsed time everywhere.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.constants: Asymptotics are a filter, not an exact timing result.

items.prompt: Arrange the process for assessing an algorithm against constraints.

elements.text: Extract maximum input dimensions, query counts, output obligations, and memory limits.
Write the candidate algorithm's time and space expressions.
Substitute the maximum constraints to estimate work and storage.
Reject, accept provisionally, or benchmark when the estimate is near the budget.

feedback.reason: Constraint analysis connects asymptotic formulas to concrete maxima.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The workload must be defined before the candidate can be costed, and the symbolic cost must be derived before values are inserted. Substitution then turns growth into an estimated operation and byte count. Only that evidence supports rejection, provisional acceptance with margin, or a benchmark decision.

items: Extract maximum input dimensions, query counts, output obligations and memory limits.
Derive the candidate's complete time and space expressions.
Substitute all independent maxima and convert storage to bytes where possible.
Reject decisive overruns, accept only with margin, or benchmark a near-boundary case.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Do not choose a budget verdict before deriving and substituting the complete workload. That reverses evidence and conclusion.

items.prompt: Arrange the analysis of a repeated-query workload.

elements.text: Compare P(n) + q·Q(n), memory, and update costs with the workload budget.

feedback.reason: Fast query time is meaningful only inside the total workload.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Separate the one-time construction P(n) from the per-query cost Q(n). Multiplying Q(n) by q captures all requested queries, after which P(n) + q·Q(n) can be compared with alternatives. Update maintenance, memory and output remain additional terms when the workload includes them.

items: Identify the one-time preprocessing cost P(n).
Identify the cost Q(n) of one query under the maintained representation.
Multiply by the maximum query count to obtain q·Q(n).
Compare P(n) + q·Q(n), update work and memory with the full workload budget.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: A low Q(n) does not justify preprocessing by itself. The break-even point depends on q and on whether the data remains valid between queries.

items.prompt: Arrange the analysis of a two-dimensional candidate cost O(nm).

elements.text: Keep n and m as separate constrained dimensions.
Estimate the product and per-pair work.
Compare the result with time and memory budgets.

feedback.reason: Collapsing dimensions too early can hide the real maximum product.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Keep n and m separate so their independent maxima and asymmetry remain visible. After substitution, multiply them because every item in one dimension is paired with every item in the other. Only then add the actual per-pair work and compare both the time count and any product-sized storage with their budgets.

items: Preserve n and m as independent constrained dimensions.
Compute n·m and include the work or storage performed per pair.
Compare the resulting operation and byte counts with the stated budgets.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Do not replace O(nm) with O(n²) unless the constraints actually establish the same bound for both dimensions; the original formula conveys more information.

items.prompt: For n = 200,000, estimate the dominant operation count of O(n log2 n) and whether it fits an abstract 100,000,000-operation budget.
constraints: Use log2(200,000) ≈ 18 and ignore constant factors.

feedback.reason: Multiplying 200,000 by about 18 gives roughly 3.6 million dominant units.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

log2 200,000 lies between 17 and 18 because 2^17 = 131,072 and 2^18 = 262,144. Using 18 gives 200,000 · 18 = 3,600,000 dominant units. This is about 28 times below the abstract 100,000,000-unit budget, so it passes the first filter but still needs constant, memory and implementation review.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: The answer is an estimate, not an exact instruction count: logarithm base and hidden work change constants but not the comfortable margin in this abstract model.

items.prompt: For n = 30,000, estimate the dominant count of an O(n²) algorithm and whether it fits an abstract 100,000,000-operation budget.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Substitution gives 30,000 · 30,000 = 900,000,000 dominant operations. Dividing by the 100,000,000-unit budget gives a factor of nine. Because the dominant count alone already overruns the budget, normal overhead only strengthens the rejection; a different algorithmic bound is required under this model.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: A ninefold gap is more than a tiny boundary uncertainty, but the conclusion still belongs explicitly to the abstract unit model rather than universal wall-clock time.

items.prompt: For n = 25, estimate the number of subset masks 2^n and whether one O(1)-work pass over all masks fits an abstract 100,000,000-operation budget.

feedback.reason: The mask count is about 33.6 million.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The enumeration visits 2^25 = 33,554,432 masks. With the prompt's O(1) work per mask, the dominant estimate is the same 33.6 million units, below the 100 million budget. If decoding instead scanned all 25 positions, the count would become about 839 million; returning all subsets would also impose enormous output storage.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: State count alone decides only the explicitly O(1)-per-state visitor. Never transfer that verdict to materialization or a more expensive loop body.

items.prompt: A workload has n = 100,000 records and q = 100,000 queries. Preprocessing costs O(n), and every query costs O(log2 n). Estimate dominant units and budget fit for a 100,000,000-operation budget.
constraints: Use log2(100,000) ≈ 17 and ignore constant factors.

feedback.reason: The estimate is 100,000 + 100,000·17 ≈ 1.8 million.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

For n = 100,000, log2 n is about 17. Preprocessing contributes 100,000 units and the queries contribute 100,000 · 17 = 1,700,000, so total dominant work is about 1,800,000. That is well below the 100 million-unit budget under the stated model, before constants and memory are reviewed.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Do not compare one O(log n) query with the budget. The workload asks for q queries, so q multiplies that term while preprocessing is added once.
